Bulk data staging and exfiltration via MEGA / rclone AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Scattered Spider's documented exfiltration tooling — rclone and MEGA clients, plus password-protected archive creation with 7-Zip/WinRAR — used to stage and move copied corporate data before extortion. Directly supports the article's account of intruders copying a retailer's data and demanding ~$8M. Rationale: rclone and MEGA (megacmd/MEGAsync) are explicitly named Scattered Spider exfil tools in CISA AA23-320A; pairing them with password-protected archive flags (-hp/-p/-mx) keys the article's 'copied its data' claim to concrete, rare-in-user-space binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT team legitimately using rclone for sanctioned cloud backup/migration
  • Developers or users making password-protected 7-Zip/WinRAR archives for routine transfers
  • Backup software invoking Compress-Archive in scheduled jobs
  • A user with a personal MEGAsync install syncing non-corporate files
  • DevOps pipelines archiving build artifacts with -mx compression
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("<sanctioned backup/migration operators>") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("<approved backup agent>.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the command line for the remote target (rclone 'mega:'/'remote:' config, archive output path) and correlate with DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections to mega.nz / user.mega.co.nz. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and block MEGA/rclone destinations at the proxy/firewall; preserve the staged archive for scoping. 3) Hunt: identify which shares/DBs were read before the archive, check for the same tool on other hosts, and review the initiating account for a preceding help-desk reset or anomalous sign-in.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("rclone.exe","megacmd.exe","megasync.exe","mega.exe")
    or (FileName in~ ("7z.exe","7za.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any (" a "," -hp"," -p ","-mx"))
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Compress-Archive")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend Proc = tolower(NewProcessName)
| where Proc has_any ("\\rclone.exe","\\megacmd.exe","\\megasync.exe","\\mega.exe")
    or (Proc has_any ("\\7z.exe","\\7za.exe","\\winrar.exe","\\rar.exe") and CommandLine has_any (" a "," -hp"," -p ","-mx"))
    or (Proc has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "Compress-Archive")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scattered Spider Data Exfiltration Tooling (rclone/MEGA/archive)
id: 7f3c1e2a-8b4d-4c6e-9a1f-2d5b6c7e8f90
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of rclone, MEGA clients or password-protected archive creation used by Scattered Spider for bulk data staging and exfiltration.
references:
  - https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/19-year-old-scattered-spider-suspect.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1567.002
  - attack.t1560.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_tools:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\rclone.exe'
      - '\megacmd.exe'
      - '\megasync.exe'
      - '\mega.exe'
  selection_archive:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\7z.exe'
      - '\7za.exe'
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - ' -hp'
      - ' -p '
      - '-mx'
  condition: selection_tools or selection_archive
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\rclone.exe OR *\\Rclone.exe OR *\\megacmd.exe OR *\\MEGAcmd.exe OR *\\megasync.exe OR *\\MEGAsync.exe OR *\\mega.exe) OR (@Image:(*\\7z.exe OR *\\7za.exe OR *\\winrar.exe OR *\\WinRAR.exe OR *\\rar.exe) AND @CommandLine:(* a * OR *\-hp* OR *\-mx*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\(rclone|megacmd|megasync|mega)\.exe$/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(7z|7za|winrar|rar)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\s(a|-hp|-p|-mx)/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/Compress-Archive/i)
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as Cmds min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("rclone.exe","megacmd.exe","megasync.exe","mega.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("7z.exe","7za.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("* a *","*-hp*","*-p *","*-mx*")) OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Compress-Archive*")) AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as Cmds min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("rclone.exe","megacmd.exe","megasync.exe","mega.exe") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("7z.exe","7za.exe","winrar.exe","rar.exe") AND Processes.process IN ("* a *","*-hp*","*-p *","*-mx*")) OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Compress-Archive*")) AND NOT Processes.user IN ("*$") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - firstTime
Adversary lurking in incident-response chat tools and calls AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts the article's distinctive Scattered Spider tradecraft: once inside, intruders lurk in the victim's collaboration tools and join breach-response meetings to watch defenders. Flags an account reading/listing messages across an unusually large number of distinct Teams channels/chats in a short window — collection of IR chatter rather than normal use. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's specific claim that intruders 'lurk in a company's chat tools and join the calls it holds to respond to the breach'; a per-account hourly fan-out across many Teams objects is an abnormal collection pattern distinct from routine messaging. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1213.005 T1580
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Compliance/eDiscovery or DLP tooling enumerating Teams content under a service account
  • A community manager or exec assistant who legitimately monitors many channels
  • Teams admin performing a migration or bulk export
  • Automated bot/connector indexing messages for search
  • New employee catching up across many onboarding channels on day one
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !in~ ("<eDiscovery/compliance service accounts>","<Teams admin accounts>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the account is a sanctioned compliance/admin/bot identity; review which channels were accessed — flag any named 'incident', 'IR', 'breach', or exec crisis channels. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, revoke Teams sessions, disable the account, and move breach-response coordination to an out-of-band channel the adversary cannot see. 3) Hunt: correlate the account with a preceding help-desk MFA reset or anomalous sign-in, and check for guest/external members recently added to IR channels.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType in ("MessagesListed","MessageRead","ChatRetrieved","MeetingParticipantDetail")
| summarize DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectId), Ops = count(), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctObjects >= 15   // reading across >=15 channels/chats in an hour = harvesting
| order by DistinctObjects desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in ("MessagesListed","MessageRead","ChatRetrieved","MeetingParticipantDetail","MemberAdded")
| summarize DistinctChannels = dcount(ObjectId), Ops = count(), OpSet = make_set(Operation, 10) by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctChannels >= 15
| order by DistinctChannels desc
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:

External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.

Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")

    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium

ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

| sort - files

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Machine that pulled compromised easy-day-js npm package (node_modules write) · [LLM] easy-day-js self-deleting postinstall dropper temp artifacts (.pkg_history/.pkg_logs) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] easy-day-js dropper C2 beacon to Sapphire Sleet Hostwinds infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] easy-day-js second-stage infostealer reading browser secrets & crypto-wallet extensions via node
Machine that pulled compromised easy-day-js npm package (node_modules write) AIInstallation High
Identifies every developer laptop or CI runner that installed the malicious easy-day-js typosquat by detecting file writes into a node_modules\easy-day-js\ directory by a package manager. This directly answers the article's 'which machine pulled the compromised package' question and scopes the blast radius of the @mastra supply-chain compromise. Rationale: Anchors on the exact malicious package path node_modules\easy-day-js\ named in the article and confirmed by Microsoft/JFrog/Socket; any write there means that host resolved and installed the poisoned dependency, which is the precise blast-radius scoping signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally installing easy-day-js in a sandbox for analysis
  • An internal mirror/artifact-cache pre-fetching the package for quarantine before the removal
  • A CI job replaying an old lockfile that still references the malicious version during remediation testing
  • A developer restoring a git branch created before the compromise was disclosed
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "quarantine" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("malwareanalysis","sandbox")
Response runbook
1) Triage: from the hit, note DeviceName + account and pull the exact easy-day-js version written (check package.json under the folder); anything resolving 1.11.22 is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network, kill node/npm processes, and delete the node_modules\easy-day-js tree; rotate any npm/registry tokens and cloud creds that lived on that host. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 on the same DeviceName for outbound connections to 23.254.164.92/123 and for .pkg_history/.pkg_logs temp artifacts to confirm second-stage execution.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","npx.cmd","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","node")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Files=make_set(FileName, 20), any(SHA256) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules/easy-day-js" or TargetFilePath has @"node_modules\easy-day-js"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","pnpm","yarn","npx")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Files=make_set(TargetFileName, 20) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by LastSeen desc

easy-day-js dropper C2 beacon to Sapphire Sleet Hostwinds infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections from a package-manager/node process to the confirmed easy-day-js command-and-control hosts 23.254.164.92:8000 (payload delivery) and 23.254.164.123:443 (RAT C2). Presence of this traffic confirms the postinstall dropper executed and reached its second stage. Rationale: The two IPs, ports (8000/443) and /24 are confirmed by Microsoft and JFrog as the easy-day-js payload-delivery and RAT C2 endpoints; direct IP hits are unambiguous second-stage confirmation and near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://www.ox.security/blog/easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-hits-mastra-ai-in-npm/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or IR team actively sandbox-detonating the sample and letting it beacon
  • A honeypot/deception host deliberately allowed to reach the C2
  • Perimeter proxy/EDR test traffic validating that the block rule works
  • Shared-hosting neighbour on 23.254.164.0/24 unrelated to the campaign (mitigated by matching the two exact IPs, not the /24)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sandbox","detonation") or DeviceName has "honeypot")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — node.exe/npm during an install window strongly confirms true positive; capture RemotePort (8000=stage-2 fetch, 443=RAT beacon). 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.92 and 23.254.164.123 at the perimeter, isolate the host, and terminate the beaconing process. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for connections to 23.254.164.0/24 and correlate with UC1 node_modules\easy-day-js writes; rotate every credential/token that resided on beaconing hosts (assume infostealer collection succeeded).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js self-deleting postinstall dropper temp artifacts (.pkg_history/.pkg_logs) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the .pkg_history / .pkg_logs marker files the easy-day-js dropper writes to the temp directory, and the self-delete pattern of a dropped .js payload during an npm install. These artifacts survive the dropper's evidence-erasure and pinpoint hosts where the payload actually executed. Rationale: The .pkg_history/.pkg_logs temp artifacts are named explicitly in the StepSecurity and Microsoft analyses as dropper leftovers; because the dropper self-deletes the payload, these marker files are the durable execution evidence and are extremely unlikely to occur benignly. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated tool coincidentally using a .pkg_history dotfile in temp (rare — validate the initiating process is node/npm)
  • IR analysts re-detonating the sample and regenerating the markers
  • A restored disk image from a compromised machine replaying the files without live execution
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is node/npm and check the file's parent folder for a recently-deleted .js payload (correlate with DeviceFileEvents ActionType=FileDeleted on the same host). 2) Contain: isolate the host and preserve the temp directory for forensics before wiping node_modules. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 for C2 beacons and UC4 for browser/wallet data access on the same DeviceName to determine whether the infostealer stage ran and exfiltrated.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("node.exe","npm.cmd","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ (".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","pnpm","yarn")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js second-stage infostealer reading browser secrets & crypto-wallet extensions via node AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a node process (the easy-day-js second-stage payload) accessing browser credential stores and cryptocurrency-wallet extension data. The recovered payload is a cross-platform infostealer targeting browser databases and 160+ wallet extensions, so node touching Chrome/Edge/Brave/Firefox 'Login Data'/'Local State' or wallet extension folders is a strong collection signal. Rationale: JFrog/Microsoft describe the recovered stage-2 as a Node-based cross-platform infostealer parsing browser databases and 160+ crypto-wallet extensions; node.exe reading Chrome/Edge 'Login Data'/'Local State' or Local Extension Settings is anomalous for a build tool and captures the collection stage this campaign is financially motivated to reach. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Electron/VS Code or other node-based desktop apps legitimately reading their own Chromium 'Local State' profile
  • Browser-automation frameworks (Puppeteer/Playwright) driven by node accessing profile data during tests
  • A backup/sync agent implemented in node copying user profile directories
  • Password-manager browser-import tooling built on node
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Microsoft VS Code\" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","electron")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the node process lineage — a node spawned by npm/postinstall or from a temp .js path is malicious, whereas a signed Electron app path is likely benign; correlate the DeviceName with UC1/UC2 hits. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force-reset all browser-saved credentials and any crypto-wallet seed/keys for the affected user; revoke cloud/SSO sessions. 3) Hunt: check UC2 for outbound beacons to 23.254.164.123:443 (exfil channel) and review proxy logs for large POSTs from the host to confirm data left the environment.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where (FileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","Cookies","Web Data"))
     or FolderPath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Local Extension Settings", "Local Extension Settings", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\", @"\BraveSoftware\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\", @"\Chromium\")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Targets=make_set(FolderPath, 30) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where (TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","Cookies","Web Data")) or TargetFilePath has "Local Extension Settings"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("Google/Chrome","Microsoft/Edge","BraveSoftware","Mozilla/Firefox","Chromium",@"Google\Chrome",@"Microsoft\Edge")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Targets=make_set(TargetFilePath, 30) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc

Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or SHA1 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or MD5 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

    ( DeviceProcessEvents

        | where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or SHA1 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or MD5 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5")

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "b73de25c053c3225a077738a1fcbd9ca6966d7b3cd6f5494a30f0aa0eae55c7e", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Multiple @immobiliarelabs Backstage Plugins Compromised on npm

StepSecurity
2026-07-01 12 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Compromised versions run a malicious payload at npm install time through a binding.gyp node-gyp hook, harvesting credentials from sources like GitHub Actions secrets, cloud provider keys, and package registry tokens, while trying to persist in AI coding assistant configs. Static analysis of version 2.1.2 against the clean 2.1.1 release revealed a new 5 MB index.js and an added binding.gyp, both absent from earlier releases.

Phantom Gyp binding.gyp install-time payload execution (Miasma npm worm) AIInstallation High
Hunts the GYP command-expansion shell invocation that the Miasma/Phantom Gyp worm plants in binding.gyp to run the 5 MB index.js during node-gyp configure, bypassing scripts.postinstall monitoring. The exact source line is '<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)', so a process command line carrying both 'node index.js' and 'echo stub.c' is the worm firing. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim binding.gyp source string '<!(node index.js > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo stub.c)' from the article; the 'node index.js' + 'echo stub.c' pairing is unique to the Phantom Gyp configure-step trick and not a legitimate gyp pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/ • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native addon packages whose binding.gyp uses node-based command expansion (rare; almost never invokes a bare index.js with echo stub.c)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox
  • CI job intentionally re-running the malicious tarball for analysis
  • A developer's own gyp build script that happens to echo a stub source file
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent chain (npm/node-gyp/sh) and identify which @immobiliarelabs (or other) package was being installed; confirm a 5 MB index.js + binding.gyp exist in that package dir. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, revoke any tokens that were live in that session (GitHub, npm, cloud), and rotate CI secrets exposed to the job. 3) Hunt: search the same host for a Bun binary in temp, IMDS (169.254.169.254) hits, and writes to AI-assistant configs (.claude/settings.json etc.); pivot org-wide on the affected package@version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("node index.js", "echo stub.c")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("node index.js", "echo stub.c")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime executing a temp payload spawned by node (Miasma Node.js-monitoring evasion) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the deliberate runtime switch where the Miasma loader downloads Bun (bun-v1.3.13) and runs the decrypted credential-harvester from a randomly named temp file under Bun instead of Node, to evade --require-hook security tooling. A bun process whose parent is node/npm/node-gyp/sh and that executes a file from /tmp or /var/folders is the second stage. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit detail that the loader downloads Bun (bun-v1.3.13) and executes the decrypted main payload from a randomly named temp file under Bun specifically to dodge Node's --require interception; node-parent + bun-child + temp path is the distinguishing shape. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/miasma-malware-uses-binding-gyp-and-bun/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/miasma-supply-chain-attack-targeting-redhat-npm-packages • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-malware-targets-npm-packages-and.html
ATT&CKT1027 T1059.007 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers who legitimately use Bun as their runtime/test-runner invoked from npm scripts
  • Bun-based build tooling executing cached transpiled output from a temp dir
  • Monorepo task runners (turbo/nx) shelling out to bun for a subpackage
  • CI images that prewarm Bun and run scratch scripts from /tmp
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the temp file path bun executed and hash it; check whether the project legitimately depends on Bun (package.json/engines) — a Bun execution with no Bun dependency declared is high-signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the bun process tree, and quarantine the temp payload before it self-deletes. 3) Hunt: correlate to a binding.gyp install in the prior 5 minutes, then look for IMDS/metadata access and AI-assistant config writes from the same session.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bun" or FileName startswith "bun-"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp","yarn","pnpm")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/","/var/tmp/") or FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/folders/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "bun"

Miasma infectHost persistence in AI coding assistant configs AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the infectHost routine that backdoors AI coding-assistant configuration files for re-execution: .claude/settings.json (SessionStart hook), .vscode/tasks.json (folderOpen), .cursor/rules/, .aider.conf.yml, and .github/copilot-instructions.md. Filters to writes performed by node/bun/npm so legit editor saves are excluded. Rationale: Directly maps the article's infectHost target list (Claude Code SessionStart hook in .claude/settings.json, VS Code folderOpen in .vscode/tasks.json, .cursor/rules, .aider.conf.yml, .github/copilot-instructions.md); requiring a node/bun writer separates the malware from legitimate IDE saves. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/immobiliarelabs-npm-packages-compromised • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1546 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer's VS Code / Cursor extension (which runs under node) legitimately writing tasks.json or rules on project open
  • Aider itself updating .aider.conf.yml during normal use
  • Dotfile-management tooling (chezmoi/yadm) restoring AI-assistant configs
  • An MCP/agent framework legitimately writing a SessionStart hook into .claude/settings.json
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code","cursor","aider") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("code","cursor"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written config and inspect the hook/command body — Miasma injects a shell/JS command into the SessionStart, folderOpen, or rules entry; benign saves contain no execution directive. 2) Contain: revert the config from version control, remove the injected hook, and isolate the host if a command was present. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo/home dir on the host for the same five config files, and check whether the SessionStart hook already fired (child processes of the AI assistant).

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.claude/settings.json", "/.vscode/tasks.json", "/.cursor/rules", "/.aider.conf.yml", "copilot-instructions.md") or FileName in~ ("settings.json","tasks.json",".aider.conf.yml","copilot-instructions.md")
| where FolderPath has_any (".claude",".vscode",".cursor",".aider.conf.yml","copilot-instructions.md")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","bun","sh","bash","dash","npm","node-gyp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")

Cloud instance-metadata harvesting from npm/node install context (Miasma credential theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Miasma harvester reaching AWS IMDS (169.254.169.254) or ECS task-metadata (169.254.170.2) from a node/bun/npm/node-gyp process — the exact endpoints the article lists for cloud credential theft. Scoped to install-tooling parents and the Bun stage so it isn't a long-running app's normal SDK traffic. Rationale: Uses the article's literal credential-source endpoints (IMDS 169.254.169.254 and ECS metadata 169.254.170.2) tied to the npm/node/Bun execution context; metadata access from package-install tooling (vs a steady-state app) is the high-fidelity differentiator. Sentinel left empty because ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-process attribution to bind the IMDS hit to node/bun. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.wiz.io/blog/miasma-supply-chain-attack-targeting-redhat-npm-packages
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1552.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js app on EC2/ECS legitimately using the AWS SDK to refresh instance-role credentials via IMDS
  • CI tooling (e.g. node-based deploy scripts) that queries instance identity at job start
  • Container health agents written in node polling task metadata
  • Infra-as-code node CLIs (CDK) resolving region/account from IMDS
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "aws-sdk" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("systemd","pm2","forever")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the calling process lineage — IMDS access from a process whose parent is npm/node-gyp/sh during a package install, or from a Bun temp process, is not normal SDK usage. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner and immediately rotate the instance-role / task-role credentials and any cloud keys reachable from that role; review CloudTrail for use of those creds from new IPs. 3) Hunt: check for follow-on reads of /proc/<Runner.Worker pid>/mem, Vault token files (/home/runner/.vault-token, /root/.vault-token, /run/secrets/VAULT_TOKEN), and .ssh/ on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun","node","npm","node-gyp","sh","bash","dash","yarn","pnpm")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "bun" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm","node-gyp","sh","bash","dash","yarn","pnpm")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

Compromised @immobiliarelabs Backstage plugin on disk (binding.gyp + index.js / known hashes) AIDelivery Medium
Inventory/IOC detection for the trojanized @immobiliarelabs/backstage-plugin-gitlab(-backend) and backstage-plugin-ldap-auth(-backend) packages. Clean releases never shipped a binding.gyp, so the presence of binding.gyp or the 5 MB index.js inside those package paths — or any file matching the three published malicious SHA256s — confirms a compromised version was installed. Rationale: Built on the article's affected-package matrix plus the three published SHA256 IOCs; a binding.gyp inside these specific Backstage plugin directories is itself anomalous because the clean 2.1.1-era releases shipped neither binding.gyp nor a 5 MB index.js. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/immobiliarelabs-npm-packages-compromised • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-6527 • https://snyk.io/blog/node-gyp-supply-chain-compromise-self-propagating-npm-worm-binding-gyp/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally staging the malicious tarball in an isolated analysis sandbox
  • A cached npm tarball retained on a build agent after remediation (already-known, low risk)
  • An offline mirror/proxy (Verdaccio/Artifactory) holding a quarantined copy for inspection
  • Hash collision is implausible — SHA256 matches are definitive
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exact package@version from the path against the affected matrix (gitlab/gitlab-backend 3.0.3–7.0.2, 1.0.1, 2.1.2; ldap-auth(-backend) 1.1.3/1.1.4–5.2.1) and check whether node-gyp executed it (install actually ran). 2) Contain: pin/roll back to a known-clean version, purge the tarball from caches and lockfiles, isolate affected build agents, and rotate every credential reachable from that host/CI job. 3) Hunt: pivot to binding.gyp execution, Bun temp execution, IMDS access, and AI-assistant config writes on the same hosts; sweep the registry/repo org for republished (worm-propagated) packages from any maintainer account touched by these runners.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FolderPath has "@immobiliarelabs" and (FolderPath has "backstage-plugin-gitlab" or FolderPath has "backstage-plugin-ldap-auth") and FileName in~ ("binding.gyp","index.js"))
    or SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108","da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707","ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetFilePath has "@immobiliarelabs" and (TargetFilePath has "backstage-plugin-gitlab" or TargetFilePath has "backstage-plugin-ldap-auth") and TargetFileName in~ ("binding.gyp","index.js"))
    or TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108","da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707","ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or SHA1 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or MD5 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or SHA1 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90") or MD5 in~ ("ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ceff7c51d70832c3ec8dd2744b606a23b3c924ef664ae23439b9b742ea154108", "da39146ef451d1b174a24d00b1e2a45cd38d54e849737f8f35333dcb22175707", "ef641e956f91d501b748085996303c96a64d67f63bfeef0dda175e5aa19cca90"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Jackson Maven typosquat C2 — beacon to fasterxml.org / 103.127.243.82 AICommand & Control High
Hunts hosts resolving or connecting to the namespace-impersonation C2 (fasterxml.org / m.fasterxml.org) or the staging IP 103.127.243.82 used by the malicious org.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind artifact to pull a Cobalt Strike beacon. Article-specific: these are typosquats of the legitimate fasterxml.com / com.fasterxml namespace, so any hit is high-fidelity. Rationale: fasterxml.org / m.fasterxml.org and 103.127.243.82:8000 are the verbatim C2 from Aikido's analysis (config.txt + svchosts.exe staging), typosquatting the real fasterxml.com — so any resolution/connection is malicious by definition. Cross-checked Aikido and cybersecuritynews/SC Media. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/maven-central-jackson-typosquatting-malware • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-infiltrated-maven-central/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/maven-central-subjected-to-typosquatted-jackson-json-library
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox or researcher detonating the sample in-house
  • Threat-intel proxy / URL-crawler pre-resolving the IOC domain
  • DNS sinkhole or RPZ responding to the domain (benign, but worth confirming sink not real resolve)
  • Internal artifact-mirror health-check probing the coordinate's declared SCM/URL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") // exclude analyst browser lookups of the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess (expect java.exe/javaw.exe from a Spring Boot app or CI runner); confirm whether the resolve led to an actual TCP connect to 103.127.243.82:8000 or :51211. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block fasterxml.org / m.fasterxml.org / 103.127.243.82 at egress, and pull the build's dependency tree for org.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind. 3) Hunt: sweep all CI runners and dev machines that resolved org.fasterxml namespace coordinates, and pivot to UC2/UC3 for dropped svchosts.exe / payload.bin and the two SHA256 implants.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "fasterxml.org" or RemoteIP == "103.127.243.82"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Java/Spring drops & runs svchosts.exe (svchost masquerade) — Jackson typosquat implant AIInstallation High
Hunts the second-stage drop where the malicious JacksonSpringAutoConfiguration class writes payload.bin to temp and executes svchosts.exe (a typosquat of the legitimate svchost.exe). Article-specific via the exact filenames and the java.exe→svchosts.exe parent/child chain. Rationale: svchosts.exe (note trailing 's') is never a legitimate Windows binary and is the verbatim Windows payload name; pairing the java.exe parent with the two confirmed SHA256 implants makes this near-zero-FP. Sourced from Aikido's payload breakdown. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/maven-central-jackson-typosquatting-malware • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-infiltrated-maven-central/
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or pentester naming an unrelated test binary svchosts.exe
  • Red-team tooling intentionally masquerading as svchost
  • Unrelated commodity malware reusing the svchosts.exe name (still malicious — escalate)
  • EDR sample-replay / detonation lab running the captured artifact
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Tests\", @"\redteam\")) // suppress sanctioned test/red-team binaries
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary path (expect a temp/working dir, not System32) and parent (java.exe/javaw.exe from a Spring Boot app or CI build); validate SHA256 against the two known implant hashes. 2) Contain: kill the process, isolate the host, and quarantine svchosts.exe / payload.bin; block the C2 from UC1. 3) Hunt: search the host and peers for the hidden .idea.pid persistence marker, for beacons to 103.127.243.82:8000 / m.fasterxml.org:51211, and audit which builds resolved org.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchosts.exe"
   or SHA256 in ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f","702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "svchosts.exe"
   or (ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe") and TargetProcessName has "svchosts.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Jackson typosquat Cobalt Strike implant hash sighting (Win + macOS/Linux) AIInstallation Medium
Vector-agnostic sweep for the two confirmed implant SHA256 hashes (svchosts.exe for Windows, 'update' for macOS/Linux) dropped by the malicious jackson-databind artifact. Catches the implant even when delivered outside the java→svchosts.exe chain (e.g. pulled directly into a CI cache). Rationale: The two SHA256 are the verbatim VirusTotal-confirmed Cobalt Strike beacons (Windows svchosts.exe + macOS/Linux 'update') from Aikido's IOC list; an exact-hash match is effectively zero-FP and covers non-Windows hosts the process/network UCs miss. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/maven-central-jackson-typosquatting-malware • https://www.scworld.com/brief/maven-central-subjected-to-typosquatted-jackson-json-library
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy of the same file retaining the original hash (benign artifact of detection)
  • Malware-research repository or sample-share host storing the IOC for analysis
  • Backup/forensic image containing a previously quarantined copy
  • Sandbox detonation lab re-fetching the sample
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","CSFalconService.exe") // exclude AV/EDR quarantine writes
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process and path — distinguish an AV/EDR quarantine vault (benign) from a live drop in a build/temp dir (true positive). 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the file, and revoke any CI/cloud credentials reachable from the build that pulled jackson-databind (Cobalt Strike harvests CI secrets). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (C2 to fasterxml.org / 103.127.243.82) and UC2 (svchosts.exe execution) on the same and neighbouring hosts, and inventory every repo/runner that resolved org.fasterxml.jackson.core coordinates.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f","702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in ("8bce95ebfb895537fec243e069d7193980361de9d916339906b11a14ffded94f","702161756dfd150ad3c214fbf97ce98fdc960ea7b3970b5300702ed8c953cafd")
