ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or SHA1 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or MD5 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or SHA1 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048") or MD5 in~ ("87603ea025623b19954e460add532048")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["87603ea025623b19954e460add532048"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ARToken: Inside an EvilTokens affiliate panel targeting Microsoft 365

Cisco Talos
2026-07-01 16 use cases 12 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Talos has identified "ARToken," a phishing-as-a-service platform that targets Microsoft 365. The ARToken panel exposes 80+ API endpoints for device code phishing, Primary Refresh Token persistence, email access, BEC operations, and SharePoint exfiltration.

ATT&CKT1027 T1098.001 T1114.002 T1190 T1497.001 T1528 T1531 T1550.001 T1566 T1566.001 T1566.002 T1583.006

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ARToken vendor-impersonation phish: inbound mail failing SPF+DKIM+DMARC with pumber.png signature lure · [LLM] SharePoint tenant lookalike via .com-folding (mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com) in phishing URL · [LLM] ARToken Cloudflare Workers lure delivery: {uuid}-docviewer/onedrive/adobe2/document.workers.dev · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] EvilTokens device-code phishing API call: POST /api/device/start with clientMode broker to C2 · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] EvilTokens PRT persistence chain: /prt/setup /prt/refresh /prt/renew /prt/reacquire /prt/cookie to C2 · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint egress to ARToken C2 / phishing infrastructure (pamconj.com, workers.dev) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
ARToken vendor-impersonation phish: inbound mail failing SPF+DKIM+DMARC with pumber.png signature lure AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the ARToken initial-access email that spoofs a trusted vendor's accounts-payable contact: inbound, delivered, all three sender-auth checks (SPF, DKIM body-hash, DMARC compauth=none) failing, carrying the outstanding-invoice lure. Anchored on the article's inline signature attachment pumber.png to raise fidelity above generic auth-fail noise. Rationale: Combines the article's stated triple auth-failure (compauth=none reason=405) with the concrete inline signature attachment pumber.png and the outstanding-invoice lure theme — far higher fidelity than auth-fail alone. Reply-To vs From pivot noted by Talos is not a first-class column in the mail-security schemas, so pumber.png + full auth failure is the durable anchor.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656 T1036.005
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor whose mail server misconfigures SPF/DKIM and coincidentally attaches an image named pumber.png (extremely unlikely)
  • Marketing/newsletter senders from mis-delegated subdomains failing all three checks
  • Forwarded internal mail losing DKIM alignment
  • A genuine AP invoice thread where the vendor's DMARC broke after a DNS change
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("yourtrusteddomain.com") // maintain an allowlist of vendor domains that legitimately fail alignment post-DNS-change
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the message, confirm SenderFromAddress domain is a known vendor while SenderMailFromAddress/sending IP is unrelated, and check the Reply-To header for an off-domain redirect. 2) Contain: quarantine/soft-delete via EmailPostDeliveryEvents, block the Reply-To domain, and warn the recipient AP mailbox. 3) Hunt: search for other recipients of the same pumber.png attachment or the same sending IP, and pivot any embedded *.sharepoint.com anchor into UC 'SharePoint tenant lookalike'.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| extend AD = parse_json(AuthenticationDetails)
| where tostring(AD.SPF) =~ "fail" and tostring(AD.DKIM) =~ "fail" and tostring(AD.DMARC) =~ "fail"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "pumber.png"
    | project NetworkMessageId, SigImage = FileName
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, SigImage, SenderIPv4, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| extend AD = parse_json(AuthenticationDetails)
| where tostring(AD.SPF) =~ "fail" and tostring(AD.DKIM) =~ "fail" and tostring(AD.DMARC) =~ "fail"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "pumber.png"
    | project NetworkMessageId, SigImage = FileName
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, SigImage, SenderIPv4, NetworkMessageId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint tenant lookalike via .com-folding (mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com) in phishing URL AIDelivery High
Detects the ARToken redirect trick where the visible anchor shows the vendor's real tenant (mononapfp.sharepoint.com) but the href targets an attacker tenant that folds the vendor's '.com' into the tenant label (mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com), inheriting SharePoint's clean reputation. Flags the concrete IOC plus the generic tenant-name-ending-in-'com' folding pattern. Rationale: Uses the exact attacker tenant mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com from the article plus the generalised '.com-folding' regex (tenant label ending in 'com' before .sharepoint.com) that captures the evasion class. Because the destination is still a real sharepoint.com host, reputation-based controls miss it — the tenant-label anomaly is the only reliable signal.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate company whose tenant name genuinely ends in 'com' (e.g. brand called 'Xcom' → xcom.sharepoint.com)
  • Internal users legitimately collaborating with a partner tenant that happens to match the pattern
  • Security-team detonation/sandbox traffic to the lookalike during investigation
  • Safe Links rewrite pre-fetch resolving the domain without a real user click
Suppression filter
| where Name !in~ ("xcom.sharepoint.com") // allowlist known-legit tenants whose label ends in 'com'
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the recipient(s), confirm the tenant label is not a real customer tenant (compare against your SharePoint external-sharing partner list), and pull the source email/anchor text. 2) Contain: block *com.sharepoint.com lookalikes at the proxy/URL filter for the specific tenant, revoke any Safe Links click-through, and force sign-out for users who clicked. 3) Hunt: correlate the resolving hosts to device-code auth (UC3) and any subsequent AAD sign-in from a new IP/device within 30 minutes.
EmailUrlInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where UrlDomain endswith ".sharepoint.com"
| where UrlDomain =~ "mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com" or UrlDomain matches regex @"(?i)^[a-z0-9-]+com\.sharepoint\.com$"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | project NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith ".sharepoint.com"
| where Name =~ "mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com" or Name matches regex @"(?i)^[a-z0-9-]+com\.sharepoint\.com$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SharePoint Tenant Lookalike via .com-Folding (ARToken)
id: 8f2b1c44-6d7e-4a19-9b2f-1c3d5e7a9b01
description: DNS resolution of a SharePoint tenant whose label ends in 'com' immediately before .sharepoint.com, a domain-folding lookalike used by the ARToken/EvilTokens phishing kit to impersonate a vendor tenant.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/07
tags:
  - attack.t1566.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection_ioc:
    query: 'mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com'
  selection_pattern:
    query|re: '(?i)^[a-z0-9-]+com\.sharepoint\.com$'
  condition: selection_ioc or selection_pattern
level: high
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(?i)([a-z0-9-]+com\.sharepoint\.com|mononapfpcom\.sharepoint\.com)$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com" OR DNS.query="*com.sharepoint.com") by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| regex query="^[a-z0-9-]+com\.sharepoint\.com$"
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="mononapfpcom.sharepoint.com" OR DNS.query="*com.sharepoint.com") by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`

| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
EvilTokens device-code phishing API call: POST /api/device/start with clientMode broker to C2 AIExploitation High
Hunts the ARToken/EvilTokens device-code phishing exchange on web-proxy telemetry: a POST to /api/device/start against attacker C2 (spx.pamconj.com) carrying the non-standard clientMode:"broker" body used to drive Microsoft's WAM broker flow for MFA-bypass token capture. This is the credential-access request that precedes victim token theft. Rationale: The article documents the exact API contract (POST /api/device/start, clientMode:"broker") matching the Sekoia-documented EvilTokens C2, and names spx.pamconj.com as the C2 host. Path + host together are high-fidelity and platform-specific to this kit. Detection lives on proxy/SWG telemetry (Defender endpoint cannot see the URL path), so defender_kql is intentionally empty; endpoint DNS to the same host is covered by the C2-egress UC.
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002 T1078.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal app that coincidentally exposes an /api/device/start route on a non-pamconj host (excluded by the host filter)
  • Security research/detonation of the kit from a sanctioned sandbox
  • Proxy log replay/testing
  • URL-scanner pre-fetch of the endpoint
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify SrcUsername/SrcIpAddr, confirm the destination is attacker-controlled (spx.pamconj.com / *pamconj.com), and check the user's AAD SigninLogs for a device-code (deviceCode) authentication within minutes. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken / conditional-access session revoke), disable the account if a token was issued, and block *.pamconj.com. 3) Hunt: pivot to the PRT-lifecycle UC for /prt/* calls from the same host and to any new device registration on the account.

| where DstHostname has "pamconj.com" or Url has "pamconj.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpMethod, Url, DstHostname, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EvilTokens PRT persistence chain: /prt/setup /prt/refresh /prt/renew /prt/reacquire /prt/cookie to C2 AIInstallation High
Hunts the Primary Refresh Token persistence lifecycle that Sekoia flagged as EvilTokens' core differentiator, reproduced in ARToken: web requests to /prt/setup, /prt/refresh, /prt/renew, /prt/reacquire and /prt/cookie against the pamconj.com C2. These calls maintain persistent, MFA-immune access to a compromised Microsoft 365 identity. Rationale: Uses the five named PRT endpoints and the pamconj.com C2 host from the article — the exact persistence chain Sekoia documented for EvilTokens. Requiring the pamconj.com host alongside /prt/* removes any chance of colliding with legitimate internal token services. Path-level signal is proxy-only, so defender_kql is empty by design.
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal identity-service using a /prt/ path on a non-pamconj host (excluded by host filter)
  • Sanctioned red-team emulating EvilTokens PRT flows
  • Proxy log testing/replay
  • Reverse-proxy health checks hitting a /prt/ route on unrelated infrastructure
Response runbook
1) Triage: map SrcUsername to an AAD identity, confirm the C2 host, and review AAD AuditLogs for a 'Register device'/'Add registered owner' event and AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs refresh-token reuse for that user. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens, delete any attacker-registered device object, disable the account, and block *.pamconj.com. 3) Hunt: enumerate mailbox inbox-rule creation (forwarding/hiding) and SharePoint file access for the account, and search for other users hitting the same /prt/* C2.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname has "pamconj.com" or Url has "pamconj.com"
| where Url has_any ("/prt/setup","/prt/refresh","/prt/renew","/prt/reacquire","/prt/cookie")
| summarize DistinctPrtEndpoints = dcount(Url), Endpoints = make_set(Url, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname
| order by LastSeen desc

ARToken Cloudflare Workers lure delivery: {uuid}-docviewer/onedrive/adobe2/document.workers.dev AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoint navigation/DNS to the ARToken phishing lure domains served from Cloudflare Workers with the kit's UUID-prefixed themed subdomains (docviewer, onedrive, adobe2, document). These pages host the seven-layer client-side anti-bot gate before delivering the device-code capture flow. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named Cloudflare Workers lure patterns ({uuid}-docviewer/-onedrive/-adobe2.workers.dev) plus the concrete IOC clear90489058903-document.workers.dev. The UUID-prefixed themed subdomain is the kit's fingerprint; the seven-layer anti-bot logic itself lives in the served JS (not in standard logs), so we detect the delivery domain that hosts it.
ATT&CKT1102 T1497 T1027
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers/QA hitting their own *.workers.dev deployments whose subdomain coincidentally contains 'document' or 'onedrive'
  • SaaS products that host document viewers on Cloudflare Workers
  • Security sandbox detonation of the lure
  • URL-scanner/Safe-Links pre-fetch resolving the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-dev") // exclude known developer/CI accounts that deploy to workers.dev
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user, confirm the workers.dev subdomain matches the UUID-prefix + theme fingerprint, and check whether a device-code auth or *.sharepoint.com lookalike followed on the same host. 2) Contain: block the specific workers.dev FQDN (and add a watch for the {uuid}-theme pattern), and warn the user; revoke tokens if auth followed. 3) Hunt: baseline all first-seen *.workers.dev resolutions org-wide (leftanti against 30-day baseline) and correlate to the pamconj.com C2 UCs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)[a-f0-9-]+-(docviewer|onedrive|adobe2|document)\.workers\.dev" or RemoteUrl has "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name matches regex @"(?i)[a-f0-9-]+-(docviewer|onedrive|adobe2|document)\.workers\.dev" or Name =~ "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint egress to ARToken C2 / phishing infrastructure (pamconj.com, workers.dev) AICommand & Control High
Domain-level net for any host resolving or connecting to ARToken command-and-control infrastructure: the pamconj.com family (pamconj.com, dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com) and the known Cloudflare Workers lure clear90489058903-document.workers.dev. This is the catch-all C2/exfil indicator across DNS and network telemetry. Rationale: Uses the article's pre-extracted C2 IOCs verbatim (pamconj.com, dashboard-bl.pamconj.com, spx.pamconj.com, clear90489058903-document.workers.dev). Fixed the prior validation error by pivoting Sentinel to DnsEvents.Name (a real column) instead of the nonexistent DnsEvents.IPAddresses. Named-domain contact is directly attributable and low-FP.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst or sandbox intentionally resolving the C2 during investigation
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment/validation tooling touching the IOCs
  • Passive-DNS or scanner appliances resolving the domain
  • Sinkholed domain (post-takedown) resolving to a benign park IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" // exclude security tooling and machine-account enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/process (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) that made the request and confirm it isn't a sanctioned TI/sandbox tool. 2) Contain: isolate the host if a user browser/Office process initiated it, block *.pamconj.com and the workers.dev FQDN at DNS/proxy, and revoke tokens for any associated user. 3) Hunt: pivot to the device-code (/api/device/start) and PRT (/prt/*) UCs for the same host/user, and sweep the org for other resolvers of pamconj.com.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl contains "pamconj.com" or RemoteUrl has "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name endswith "pamconj.com" or Name =~ "clear90489058903-document.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)

    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort

| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

Phantom Squatting Uses AI-Hallucinated Domains for Phishing and Malware

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 10 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Large language models keep inventing web addresses that do not exist. Attackers have started buying those made-up domains before anyone else can, then hosting phishing pages on them to catch traffic that AI tools point their way. Palo Alto Networks'&nbsp;Unit 42&nbsp;calls the trick phantom squatting, and its new research shows it is already happening in the wild. The reason it matters is

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP / postal-service APK file hash on endpoint · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Victim traffic to Montana Empire phishing-kit endpoints (/mentalite.php, /panel_track.php, /verify_api.php, /letgovip.zip) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP / postal-service APK file hash on endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoints that write or download the two Unit 42-confirmed Phantom Squatting artifacts: the Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP (SHA256 eb07edaa…, 7,958,528 bytes) and the malicious postal-service Android APK (SHA256 2202a30d…, 12,649,472 bytes). Article-specific because it pins exact corroborated hashes rather than a generic 'suspicious download' pattern. Rationale: Uses the two SHA256 hashes and exact file sizes (7,958,528-byte ZIP kit, 12,649,472-byte APK) published in Unit 42's primary report and cross-checked against the hendryadrian mirror; exact-hash matching is inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://x.com/Unit42_Intel/status/2041879323963982303 • https://www.hendryadrian.com/phantom-squatting-ai-hallucinated-domains-as-a-software-supply-chain-vector/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/IR analyst intentionally downloading the sample from MalwareBazaar/VirusTotal for analysis
  • Automated malware-detonation sandbox host writing the sample to disk
  • Threat-intel platform syncing IOC sample repositories to a research share
  • Red-team exercise staging the kit for a phishing-simulation replica
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("IR-SANDBOX01","MALWARE-LAB01") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vmtoolsd.exe","cuckoo.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the hash match and inspect FileOriginUrl/InitiatingProcess to determine if the file arrived via browser download, email attachment, or file share, and whether the host is an analyst/sandbox box (expected) or a standard user endpoint (unexpected). Step 2 — Contain: on a non-analyst endpoint, isolate the device, quarantine the file, and reset any credentials/payment data entered on the associated phishing domain. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on FileOriginUrl/RemoteUrl to identify the phantom domain, then sweep the org for other hosts contacting that host or the kit's PHP endpoints (see companion UC), and check EmailAttachmentInfo for the same SHA256.

| where SHA256 in ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd","2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd","2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Victim traffic to Montana Empire phishing-kit endpoints (/mentalite.php, /panel_track.php, /verify_api.php, /letgovip.zip) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts endpoints whose browser or an AI agent reaches the distinctive server-side paths of the Montana Empire kit, where card numbers, IBANs, national IDs and OTPs are captured and relayed to the operator's Telegram panel. Article-specific because it keys on the kit's actual PHP filenames rather than generic phishing heuristics. Rationale: Uses the four distinctive kit paths (/mentalite.php, /panel_track.php, /verify_api.php, /letgovip.zip) enumerated in Unit 42's Montana Empire teardown; /mentalite.php and /letgovip.zip are highly non-generic, so co-occurrence with the two /*_api endpoints is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://x.com/Unit42_Intel/status/2041879323963982303
ATT&CKT1056.003 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal or SaaS app that happens to expose a generically-named /verify_api.php or /panel_track.php endpoint
  • Security scanner or web crawler enumerating .php paths across many hosts
  • Red-team phishing-simulation infrastructure mirroring the kit paths
  • DAST/pentest tooling probing arbitrary PHP endpoints during an authorized assessment
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/mentalite.php","/letgovip.zip") or (RemoteUrl has_any ("/panel_track.php","/verify_api.php") and RemoteIPType == "Public")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the RemoteUrl/DstHostname is an external, recently-registered domain impersonating a postal service, bank, or betting brand (not an internal app), and check which user/process initiated the request. Step 2 — Contain: block the domain/IP at proxy and DNS, and if the user reached /panel_track.php or /verify_api.php, treat any payment card, IBAN, national ID, or OTP they entered as compromised and initiate card reissue / account lockdown. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the destination host to find all other org users who touched it, correlate with the file-hash UC for the dropped APK, and query newly-observed domains resolving to the same IP to surface sibling phantom domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/mentalite.php","/panel_track.php","/verify_api.php","/letgovip.zip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("/mentalite.php","/panel_track.php","/verify_api.php","/letgovip.zip")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, Url, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenClaw agent runtime exfiltrating to Telegram Bot API AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts an OpenClaw/agent interpreter process (node/python/deno/bun) resolving or connecting to api.telegram.org — the C2/exfil channel used by the malicious ClawHub skill cluster (polymarketbtc family) to ship stolen tokens and crypto keys out. Article-specific because it ties the agent runtime, not a browser, to Telegram Bot API egress. Rationale: api.telegram.org / t.me are the concrete C2 domains for the polymarketbtc ClawHub skill cluster (krajekisbtc) that exfiltrated tokens/keys; scoping the egress to agent interpreters (node/python/deno/bun) rather than browsers is what makes it article-specific and low-noise. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/researchers-find-341-malicious-clawhub.html • https://cofense.com/blog/weaponizing-telegram-bots-how-threat-actors-exfiltrate-credentials • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/
ATT&CKT1567 T1102.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using a legitimate node/python Telegram bot library for a sanctioned notification bot
  • CI/CD runner posting build status to a corporate Telegram channel via curl
  • Security researcher testing Telegram Bot API integrations in a sandbox
  • Personal productivity script the user knowingly runs that pushes alerts to t.me
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("corp-notify-bot","ci-status") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — identify the skill/script driving the agent and whether the Telegram bot token is hardcoded; correlate to any SKILL.md or config the agent loaded in the prior 10 min. 2) Contain: kill the agent process, rotate all tokens/keys reachable from that host (Anthropic/OpenAI API keys, Slack OAuth, cloud creds, git tokens), and block api.telegram.org egress for non-approved hosts. 3) Hunt: search other hosts for the same agent runtime touching Telegram, and for reads of .env/credentials files by the same runtime.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org" or RemoteUrl has "t.me"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name endswith "telegram.org" or Name == "t.me"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell to harvest credential/token files AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts an OpenClaw/agent interpreter (node/python/deno/bun) spawning a shell whose command line touches secret stores — .env, cloud credential files, SSH keys, .npmrc, or provider API-key variables. Grounded in the article's note that agents keep tokens/keys in env vars or plain-text files alongside the agent, which malicious skills harvest via embedded bash. Rationale: The article states agents store tokens/keys in env vars or plain-text files alongside the agent and that malicious skills harvest them via embedded bash; scoping parent=agent-runtime + child=shell + a secret-store string in the cmdline is the concrete high-fidelity pivot corroborated by Snyk's OpenClaw credential-leak research. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/openclaw-skills-credential-leaks-research/ • https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate skill loading a .env for a sanctioned integration (e.g. a deployment helper reading credentials it is authorized to use)
  • Developer debugging an agent locally and grepping their own .npmrc / .env
  • DevOps automation that echoes an API-key variable name (not value) during setup
  • Package-manager install (npm/pip) that touches .npmrc as part of normal auth
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","pip install") and ProcessCommandLine has ".npmrc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full child ProcessCommandLine and the parent agent's loaded skill/config — determine whether the secret access is part of a sanctioned skill or an untrusted ClawHub skill pulled recently. 2) Contain: suspend the agent, quarantine the skill file, and rotate every credential the command referenced (cloud, git, provider API keys, Telegram/Slack tokens). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host+user for outbound connections to api.telegram.org / paste sites shortly after (join to UC1), and sweep other hosts running the same skill hash/name.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","curl.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".env","credentials","id_rsa",".ssh",".npmrc","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY","OPENAI_API_KEY","TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any (".env","credentials","id_rsa",".ssh",".npmrc","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY","OPENAI_API_KEY","TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, NewProcessId
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

The activity, per Huntress, originates from an IPv6 address range (2a0a:d683::/32) controlled by internet infrastructure provider LSHIY LLC (AS32167). "Between June 12 and June 26, the threat

Successful Azure CLI sign-in from LSHIY LLC IPv6 range (2a0a:d683::/32) — confirmed compromise AIExploitation High
Hunts for successful Entra sign-ins to the first-party Azure CLI app (04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46) originating from the LSHIY LLC attacker infrastructure (2a0a:d683::/32, AS32167/AS955). Any success from this range against this app equals a confirmed account takeover from the ongoing LSHIY password-spray campaign, so it is the sharpest post-compromise pivot. Rationale: Uses three high-fidelity article IOCs together: the Azure CLI app ID 04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46, the LSHIY LLC IPv6 range 2a0a:d683::/32 and its ASNs (32167/955), plus a success result — a combination with effectively no benign explanation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/lshiy-password-spray-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/azure-cli-password-spray-hits-at-least.html • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/5847440/unable-to-authenticate-azure-cli-for-frontdoor-con
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate user or admin whose ISP is (mis)attributed to AS32167/AS955 in the geo-IP feed
  • Corporate egress or cloud automation NAT'd through an IPv6 address that overlaps the range (unlikely — dedicated attacker infra)
  • Threat-intel/red-team validation testing intentionally sourced from the same range
  • Delayed/replayed sign-in log ingestion causing a stale success to re-surface
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the UPN, IP and app; pull the user's full SigninLogs for the prior 14 days to see the preceding failed-spray attempts and any other successful IPs. 2) Contain: Immediately revoke all refresh/access tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force a password reset, and disable the account until identity is re-verified; block 2a0a:d683::/32 at the CA named-location/IP layer. 3) Hunt: Enumerate every account with any auth (success or fail) from AS32167/AS955, review post-login Azure activity (AzureActivity, role/app-consent changes) for the compromised identity, and audit CA policies for the ROPC gap.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ApplicationId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where ipv6_is_match(IPAddress, "2a0a:d683::/32")               // LSHIY LLC (AS32167) range
| where ErrorCode == 0                                            // successful auth = compromise
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, Country, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, AuthenticationRequirement, IsInteractive, ResourceDisplayName
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AppId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where AutonomousSystemNumber in (32167, 955) or ipv6_is_match(IPAddress, "2a0a:d683::/32")   // LSHIY LLC infrastructure
| where ResultType == "0"                                 // successful sign-in = compromise
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserId, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, Location, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus, AuthenticationRequirement, IsInteractive, ResourceDisplayName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Azure CLI ROPC password spray from LSHIY LLC (2a0a:d683::/32) — high failed-auth fan-out AIExploitation High
Detects the password-spray phase: a burst of failed Entra sign-ins to the Azure CLI app from the LSHIY LLC infrastructure hitting many distinct accounts per hour. This is the article's 81M-attempt credential-spray behaviour, scoped to the attacker's app + network IOCs so it fires before a spray converts to compromise. Rationale: Combines the Azure CLI app ID, the LSHIY IPv6 range/ASNs and a >=5 distinct-account-per-hour fan-out on failures — the defining shape of the campaign's password spray (bad-password 50126 / lockout 50053) rather than a single-account brute force. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/lshiy-password-spray-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/azure-cli-password-spray-hits-at-least.html
ATT&CKT1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A broken CI/CD pipeline or SDK using stale Azure CLI credentials generating repeated 50126s (but from corporate IP, not AS32167)
  • Geo-IP misattribution folding a benign ISP into AS32167/AS955
  • Password-manager mass-rotation failures across many service accounts from one host
  • Sign-in log ingestion backfill inflating the hourly count for a single window
Response runbook
1) Triage: Review the SampleUsers set — confirm they are real tenant identities and check whether any subsequently show ResultType 0 (successful compromise) from the same range. 2) Contain: Add 2a0a:d683::/32 (and AS32167/AS955) to a CA block named-location and enable the userStrongAuthClientAuthNRequired setting to block ROPC; pre-emptively force password reset on any sprayed account confirmed to use a breached/unrotated password. 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC 'Successful Azure CLI sign-in from LSHIY' to catch conversions, and search other apps/ASNs for the same fan-out pattern (campaign spans multiple ASNs).
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ApplicationId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where ipv6_is_match(IPAddress, "2a0a:d683::/32")               // LSHIY LLC (AS32167) range
| where ErrorCode != 0                                            // failed spray attempts
| summarize FailedAttempts=count(), TargetedAccounts=dcount(AccountObjectId), SampleUsers=make_set(AccountUpn, 15), ErrorCodes=make_set(ErrorCode, 10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by bin(Timestamp, 1h), IPAddress
| where TargetedAccounts >= 5     // 5 = spray fan-out floor; single-user brute stays below
| order by FailedAttempts desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where AppId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where AutonomousSystemNumber in (32167, 955) or ipv6_is_match(IPAddress, "2a0a:d683::/32")   // LSHIY LLC infrastructure
| where ResultType != "0"                                 // failed spray attempts
| summarize FailedAttempts=count(), TargetedAccounts=dcount(UserId), SampleUsers=make_set(UserPrincipalName, 15), ResultTypes=make_set(ResultType, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h), IPAddress
| where TargetedAccounts >= 5     // 5 = spray fan-out floor; single-user brute stays below
| order by FailedAttempts desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.appDisplayName:"Microsoft Azure CLI" @properties.status.errorCode:(50126 OR 50053 OR 50055) CIDR(@network.client.ip, 2a0a:d683::/32)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as failed_attempts, dc(Authentication.user) as targeted_users, values(Authentication.user) as users, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="Microsoft Azure CLI" Authentication.action="failure" by Authentication.src, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where cidrmatch("2a0a:d683::/32", src) AND targeted_users>=5
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - failed_attempts
| tstats summariesonly=false count as failed_attempts, dc(Authentication.user) as targeted_users, values(Authentication.user) as users, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="Microsoft Azure CLI" Authentication.action="failure" by Authentication.src, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where cidrmatch("2a0a:d683::/32", src) AND targeted_users>=5
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - failed_attempts
Azure CLI ROPC sign-in bypassing Conditional Access (CA NotApplied, non-interactive) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the systemic weakness the campaign abuses: successful non-interactive Azure CLI (ROPC) sign-ins where Conditional Access was NotApplied — i.e. the legacy ROPC /token flow slipped past CAP because policy never evaluated. Catches this bypass tenant-wide regardless of source IP, surfacing exposure even from future attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Anchors on the article's core mechanism — ROPC to the Azure CLI app (04b07795-...) succeeding with ConditionalAccessStatus=notApplied — which is exactly how the campaign slipped past MFA/CAP; scoping to non-interactive + this app keeps it tied to the specific bypass rather than generic sign-ins. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/lshiy-password-spray-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/azure-cli-password-spray-hits-at-least.html
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers/automation using `az login` with username/password (ROPC) from unmanaged scripts where no CA policy targets Azure CLI
  • Service/break-glass accounts intentionally excluded from CA that use Azure CLI
  • Pipelines running Azure CLI from an agent not covered by any CA assignment
  • Tenants that simply have no CA policy scoped to the Azure CLI app (the very gap being hunted) generating expected-but-risky volume
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$" and AccountUpn !has "break-glass" and AccountUpn !has "svc-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: For each UPN, confirm whether the source IPs are corporate/known-automation or unfamiliar (cross-check against 2a0a:d683::/32 and other spray ASNs); benign ROPC from corp IPs is exposure, ROPC from unknown IPs is likely compromise. 2) Contain: Close the gap — extend CA to All Cloud Apps + All Client App types and enable userStrongAuthClientAuthNRequired to block ROPC; revoke sessions for any UPN with unfamiliar-IP ROPC success. 3) Hunt: List all identities using ROPC/Azure CLI to size migration off the legacy flow, and correlate these UPNs against the LSHIY spray failed-auth set to spot pre-compromise targeting.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ApplicationId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where ErrorCode == 0                                            // successful token issuance
| where IsInteractive == false                                    // ROPC is non-interactive
| where ConditionalAccessStatus =~ "notApplied"                   // CAP never evaluated = bypass
| summarize SignIns=count(), Countries=make_set(Country, 10), IPs=make_set(IPAddress, 15), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, AccountObjectId, ClientAppUsed
| order by SignIns desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AppId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46"   // Azure CLI first-party app
| where ResultType == "0"                                 // successful token issuance
| where ConditionalAccessStatus =~ "notApplied"          // CAP never evaluated = ROPC bypass
| summarize SignIns=count(), IPs=make_set(IPAddress, 15), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, UserId, ClientAppUsed, AppDisplayName
| order by SignIns desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

description: |

references:

logsource:

            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
